blocks.text: The result of five years of work in Southern Italy, Alessia Rollo’s book Altera Italia brings readers face to face with the region’s ancestral rituals, set in a South that, in her view, doesn’t exist in the way we imagine it.
By Gaia Squarci. Artwork by Alessia Rollo.

In Italy, the word “pagan” carries a negative charge. In mainstream eyes, like dialects, it is associated with ignorance and backwardness. Christian authority claimed the land and its traditions, stripping catharsis and collective trance of their power. Anthropologists preserved the memory of some of these rituals, but their analytical approach flattened them. In the artist’s words, “rituals cannot be explained; they must be lived.”

Alessia Rollo works with archival material as much as her own contemporary documentation, pushing back against a stereotyped image of the South as backward, superstitious and, conveniently, highly marketable. Cutting into and painting over the surface of the photographs becomes, for her, a magical act that brings these visual records back to life. The book follows the cycle of the seasons, which shapes both agricultural life and the shifts in collective behaviour.

At the heart of her work lie the most essential expressions of the human soul. Grief is one of them. Women once voiced it publicly, in rituals meant to release pain for the whole community; today it has become private, polite and shameful, “a power too feminine, too brazen and too boisterous for an industrialised country.” In recent decades, raves held in the countryside, an attempt to build community beyond society’s walls, may have taken up that role. Then they, too, were silenced: inconvenient for mass tourism.
The book Altera Italia is published by Miracoli Visivi and available for 40 Euro.
